To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the risk of clinically recognized opioid abuse/dependence among veterans using opioids is higher for individuals with a diagnosis of non-opioid substance abuse or mental health disorders and is also higher for males, younger adults, or individuals with a higher number of days supply of opioid prescriptions dispensed.

the risk of developing clinically recognized opioid abuse or dependence was higher among individuals with a non‐opioid drug abuse diagnosis, a mental health diagnosis, and a greater days’ supply of prescription opioids in 2002.
the strongest predictors of opioid abuse/ dependence among chronic opioid users are a diagnosis of non-opioid substance abuse and a diagnosis of mental health disorder.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of risk factors for clinically recognized (i. e., diagnosed) opioid dependence or abuse among chronic users of opioids.
understanding the risk factors for clinically recognized (diagnosed) opioid abuse and dependence, which are the most serious adverse outcomes associated with opioid therapy.
the risk factors for clinically recognized (diagnosed) opioid abuse/dependence among veterans who use opioids for CNCP.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the risk factors for clinically recognized (i. e., diagnosed) opioid dependence among chronic users of opioids is non‐opioid abuse, mental health disorders, age and sex, and days of opioid supplied.
there is insufficient evidence to support or refute the use of opioids in the treatment of chronic pain.

the risk for opioid abuse and dependence can be reduced by identifying and treating patients with a history of substance abuse, mental health disorders and other risk factors for opioid use disorders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
clinicians should carefully screen for substance and mental health disorders and facilitate appropriate treatment for these conditions in candidates for opioid analgesic therapy for chronic pain.
mental health disorders, particularly depression and anxiety, are the most prevalent and important risk factors for the onset of opioid abuse or dependence in chronic users of opioid analgesics.
the strongest predictors of opioid abuse/dependency were a history of non‐opioids abuse/dependence disorders and a history of mental health disorders.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the prevalence of mental disorders among chronic opioid users is high and that these mental health disorders, particularly depression and anxiety, are important predictors of opioid abuse/ dependence.
the risk factors for the abuse of prescription opioids in CNCP are not well‐understood, and that there is a need for more research on this important issue.

mental health disorders are much more common among chronic users of opioids than is non‐opioid drug abuse and that mental health disorders, not non‐opioid abuse, are a major risk factor for the development of opioid abuse and dependency among chronic users of prescription opioids.
